newsitem.title: FINLAND: Derivatives loss push Finnish oil trader into red.
newsitem.headline: Derivatives loss push Finnish oil trader into red.

text.p: A $100 million write-off on crude oil trading derivatives helped propel Finnish oil group Neste Oy to a shock January-August loss, but the company said on Friday it should end the year in profit.

Reporting a loss before extraordinaries and tax of 26 million markka ($5.7 million), compared with 1.14 billion profits in January-August 1995, Neste said it had also been hit by weak petrochemicals and lower gains from fixed assets sales.

The company said the loss included a 495 million markka write-down on crude oil derivatives trading to the end of August 1997, far bigger than derivatives losses announced in July for up to the end of 1996.
It warned on July 25 that sharply rising crude oil prices would cost it around 285 million to the end of the calendar year at that day's prices.

But the company gave few details of its trading in derivatives -- sophisticated financial instruments that allow market players to hedge their positions or speculate on prices moving in a certain direction.
No analysts polled before the result had forecast a loss for the company, which is majority state-owned.
Neste stock was marked down quite sharply in early Helsinki trading, but later improved as some analysts welcomed the decisive write-down. They later rose 1.00 to 93.00 markka.
"I assume now the slate is clean for 1997," said Jussi Hyoty, analyst at AG Private Bankers.
Neste said it had now eliminated risks linked to the derivatives contracts maturing by the end of this year and cancelled similar instruments due in 1997 and 1998.
"Neste's remaining unmatured buying and selling contracts are conventional positions, which are considerably smaller in volume than the company's own crude oil production," said Neste's report.
Chief executive Jaakko Ihamuotila told a news conference that Neste's loss was now limited and could even shrink because any further rise in crude oil prices would benefit the company.
"If crude oil prices later rise ... our own crude oil production is substantially larger than these trading volumes, so we would benefit more from a rise ... than we would suffer," he said.
Ihamuotila said the losses stemmed from the 1980s when Neste sold its stake in an unnamed oil field and simultaneously sealed a long-term purchase deal on crude produced by the field.
"This created the need for long-term control (of the risks in) this agreement," he said.
He said Neste at the end of 1995 and early 1996 had adopted "certain new instruments" which led to the losses, but declined to deail them, saying this was a "business secret."

The company -- Finland's largest by sales until the merger of forestry giants UPM and Kymmene last year -- built up considerable oil trading muscle in the 1970s and 1980s as an outlet for barter crude oil from the former Soviet Union.
Last month the company replaced the head of its trading unit and pledged to tighten up its trading procedures. ($1=4.57 Markka)
